standard.title: Landscape distribution
standard.description: the location and distribution of Australia's distinctive landscapes and significant landforms
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain water distribution at the national scale and have located water resources on maps (AC9HG7K02). They have not yet mapped the distribution of landform types or related landscape patterns across Australia.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the location and distribution of Australia's distinctive landscapes and significant landforms, including their significance to First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Locating Australian landscapes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can locate and name distinctive Australian landscapes and significant landforms on a map.
nodes.minimum_width: Students locate at least three distinctive landscapes or significant landforms on a map of Australia.
nodes.typical_width: Students represent the distribution of distinctive Australian landscapes (deserts in Central Australia, tropical rainforests in the north) and significant landforms (Uluru, Blue Mountains) on a map, describing the spatial pattern.
wider: Compare the distribution of Australian landscapes with those of another country, identifying similarities and differences in the pattern.
Investigate why certain landscape types cluster in particular parts of Australia, linking climate zones to landscape distribution.
Examine how mapping technology (satellite imagery, GIS) has changed how we document landscape distribution.
nodes.hinge_reason: Spatial location is the foundation for all comparison and significance work in Nodes 2–3. Students who cannot accurately locate landscapes will be unable to make meaningful distribution comparisons or relate First Nations connections to specific places.

response_modes.reason: Mapping and locating require repeated practice with cartographic tools. Students need to use maps actively — not just read them — before they can represent distributions confidently.

success_criteria: Accurately locates and labels at least three distinctive landscapes or significant landforms on a map of Australia.
Describes the spatial distribution pattern (e.g., deserts concentrated in the interior, rainforests in the north).

nodes.label: What makes landscapes iconic
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe what makes Australian landscapes and landforms iconic, including their distinctive visual and environmental characteristics.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least one iconic landscape or landform and explain what distinguishes it.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify and describe the characteristics that make selected Australian landscapes and landforms iconic — physical form, rarity, scale, distinctiveness — and compare the distribution of Australian landscapes with those of another country.
wider: Examine how 'iconicity' is socially constructed — what criteria make a place iconic and who decides?
Compare iconic landscape features in Australia with analogous features internationally (e.g., Australian desert vs Mongolian steppe).
Investigate how tourism industries shape and amplify the iconic status of certain landscapes.

response_modes.reason: Examining iconic landscapes across multiple contexts — different regions of Australia and internationally — prevents students from treating one example as definitively 'what iconic looks like' and builds capacity for comparative geographic thinking.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The concept of 'iconic' landscapes invites genuine critical thinking about how place value is constructed — culturally, commercially and politically. Wider students can interrogate whose values define iconicity, a line of inquiry that connects to K03.
success_criteria: Describes at least two characteristics that make a selected landscape or landform distinctive or iconic.
Compares at least one Australian landscape type with an equivalent landscape in another country.

nodes.label: Significance to First Nations Australians
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the significance of a landform important to First Nations Australians, including its name, meaning and cultural/spiritual significance.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the significance of one landform to a First Nations Australian community, including its name and meaning.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the significance of a landform important to First Nations Australians (e.g., Three Sisters/Blue Mountains, Budj Bim, Uluru-Kata Tjuta), including the names, meanings and layered significance (cultural, spiritual, ecological) that the community associates with the place.
wider: Examine how First Nations place names encode geographic and cultural knowledge about landscapes and landforms.
Compare how the same place is understood differently by First Nations communities and mainstream tourism industries.
Investigate how native title and land rights legislation intersects with the recognition of First Nations connections to iconic landscapes.

response_modes.reason: Using multiple First Nations examples — from different Country and different types of significance — prevents reduction to a single exemplar and honours the diversity of First Nations relationships to landscapes.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The layered meanings of Country/Place for First Nations Australians offer genuine conceptual depth — material, spiritual, cultural and ecological dimensions co-existing in one place. Wider exploration of this multiplicity is rich and non-trivial.
success_criteria: Names and describes a landform significant to a First Nations Australian community, including its First Nations name and meaning.
Explains at least two dimensions of significance (cultural, spiritual, ecological, historical) that the community associates with the place.
